flutamide.text: Flutamide is a prostate-cancer antiandrogen that some hair-loss communities discuss, in topical or oral form, as an off-label way to curb androgen-driven thinning and keep more hair. Its use for hair has been studied mainly in women, and forum comparisons with other antiandrogens rest on anecdote.

bicalutamide.text: Bicalutamide is a prostate-cancer antiandrogen used off-label for female pattern hair loss, and some forum users also float it for recovery after finasteride or isotretinoin. Evidence for hair is retrospective data in women; the recovery idea is based on anecdote.

cyproterone-acetate.text: Cyproterone acetate is a progestin-antiandrogen prescribed to women for hirsutism, severe acne and androgen-related hair loss, so it comes up in discussions of hormone-driven skin and hair. Its use for these conditions is established in clinical practice; appearance use in men is largely anecdotal.

latanoprost.text: Latanoprost is a glaucoma eye drop whose side effects include longer, thicker lashes and darker iris pigmentation, which is why appearance communities mention it for lashes and eye colour. The effects are documented as side effects of the medical use; cosmetic trials have not been run.

onion-juice.text: Onion juice is a folk scalp remedy that users apply hoping to regrow hair and thicken thinning areas, often mentioned alongside rosemary oil and rice water. Evidence for this use is one small trial in alopecia areata plus anecdote, rather than trials in pattern baldness.

rosemary-oil.text: Rosemary oil is used as a natural alternative to minoxidil, applied to the scalp and sometimes to brows and lashes for thicker growth. One small 2015 trial compared it with 2% minoxidil for pattern hair loss; the brow and lash uses rest on anecdote.

anastrozole.text: Anastrozole is a breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers discuss as a way to delay growth-plate closure and add height, and that TRT users discuss for oestrogen control. The height theory is untested in healthy people; its approved use is in breast cancer.

letrozole.text: Letrozole is a potent aromatase inhibitor that heightmaxxers consider for delaying growth plates, and that some users link to leanness through lowered oestrogen. Trials cover breast cancer and fertility; use for height or gains in healthy people is untested and discussed mostly on forums.

exemestane.text: Exemestane is a steroidal aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers favour as the milder option for keeping growth plates open and adding height. It is approved for breast cancer; the height use has not been tested in healthy adolescents and rests on forum reports.

tamoxifen.text: Tamoxifen is a breast-cancer SERM that bodybuilders and TRT users take to treat or prevent gynecomastia and sometimes to support muscle gain. It is used clinically for breast conditions and has been studied for male gynecomastia; the muscle-gain claims are based on anecdote.

clomiphene.text: Clomiphene is a fertility SERM that men use off-label to raise their own testosterone without injections, or to recover after steroid cycles, in pursuit of more muscle and leanness. It has some evidence in hypogonadal men; effects on looks are untested.

enclomiphene.text: Enclomiphene is the trans-isomer of clomiphene, taken by men to lift natural testosterone while preserving fertility and testicle size, and sometimes discussed for post-cycle recovery or height. It has been studied in men with secondary hypogonadism; appearance and height uses are largely untested.

nicotine.text: Nicotine, via pouches, gum or vapes, is used by some in appearance communities as an appetite suppressant to stay lean, and for focus. Trials have not tested it for leanness, and forum posters also debate effects on hair, skin and teeth.

benzoyl-peroxide.text: Benzoyl peroxide is the over-the-counter acne staple used in washes and leave-on products for clearer skin, and some users also use the wash on the body for breakouts and odor. Its acne use is backed by guidelines and decades of trials; the odor use is anecdotal.

snail-mucin.text: Snail mucin is a Korean-skincare staple used for hydration, a glowing look, fading acne marks and softening fine lines. Reviews describe small studies on hydration and scars as promising, with large clinical trials still lacking.

centella-asiatica.text: Centella asiatica, or cica, is used in calming Korean skincare products to reduce redness, help acne marks and scars heal, and support skin quality. Trials exist for wound and scar healing; evidence for anti-aging and general looks is small and mixed in quality.

bakuchiol.text: Bakuchiol is promoted as a plant-based retinol alternative for wrinkles, pigmentation and acne, favoured by people who find retinol irritating. A handful of small trials report retinol-like results with less irritation.

chain: Fewer clogged pores and dark spots
mandelic-acid.text: Mandelic acid is a large-molecule alpha-hydroxy acid used in gentle peels and serums for acne, dark spots, acne marks and photoaging, often by people with sensitive skin. Direct clinical evidence is thin, with most support coming from related acids.

tea-tree-oil.text: Tea tree oil is used topically for acne, post-shave breakouts, body odor and scalp care, and is sometimes claimed to lower testosterone. Small trials exist for acne and eyelid mites; the testosterone and shaving claims rest on anecdote.

squalane.text: Squalane is a light moisturising oil used in serums and moisturisers, and on lips and hair, to leave skin soft and supple. The smoother, hydrated feel is immediate, though trial data specific to squalane is limited.

sulfur-topical.text: Topical sulfur is an old over-the-counter option in masks, soaps and spot treatments for acne, rosacea and body breakouts, popular among people avoiding harsher actives. Rosacea has decent trial support; the acne data are thinner.

topical-finasteride.text: Topical finasteride is applied to the scalp to slow pattern hair loss while limiting systemic exposure and side effects, and is used by people who want to keep their hairline. Trials are encouraging but smaller than for the oral drug.

fluridil.text: Fluridil, sold in Europe as Eucapil, is a topical antiandrogen used for pattern hair loss by people seeking a non-systemic option. Evidence is a single small 2002 trial.

caffeine-shampoo.text: Caffeine shampoos such as Alpecin are marketed to people with thinning hair as an easy addition to a hair-loss routine. Evidence is one trial in women, with little else behind it.

tongkat-ali.text: Tongkat ali is a root extract sold as a natural testosterone booster, taken in pursuit of better muscle, leaner body composition and libido. Small trials lean positive on testosterone and mood, while broader reviews are more sceptical.

fadogia-agrestis.text: Fadogia agrestis is a podcast-popular stem extract taken, often stacked with tongkat ali, as a testosterone booster for muscle and libido. Support comes from rat studies; human trials are lacking.

shilajit.text: Shilajit is a Himalayan mineral resin taken for testosterone, energy and recovery, and sometimes for bones and collagen. One small trial supports a testosterone rise; the physique and ageing uses rest on traditional claims and anecdote.

cistanche.text: Cistanche is a Chinese tonic herb that bodybuilding forums list as a testosterone and DHT booster, used for libido, strength and recovery, including after cycles. Human trials on these uses are essentially absent.

kisspeptin.text: Kisspeptin-10 is a hypothalamic peptide that TRT users discuss as an hCG alternative to keep the testes active and to aid post-cycle recovery. Kisspeptin has been given to people in research and shown to raise LH; the TRT use has not been tested.

gonadorelin.text: Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH that TRT users take as a substitute for hCG to prevent testicular atrophy. It is established in fertility medicine and diagnostics; its use as an hCG substitute is untested, and forum posters disagree about its effectiveness.
